name: Källemo
notes: Joomla site, generic robots.txt (no bot-specific blocks). No product API, but 6 category listing pages under /en/products/{category} each server-render every item's name, designer, and image in one fetch. A 7th category, 'archive', is discontinued designs and is excluded, same treatment as Ingo Maurer's ceased models. Category label set per-folder where unambiguous (chairs/tables/shelves), left blank where a folder genuinely mixes object types (sofas-easychairs, other, limited).

name: Mizuyo
notes: robots.txt is the generic Squarespace AI-bot template (harmless, same as H. Bigeleisen/Yird), not a real block. Deferred for a different reason: the /shop listing has zero products in its server-rendered HTML (no product markup or embedded JSON - likely client-fetched or currently empty), and individual product pages (checked /kasuri-apron, /kiriko) only carry generic site-level schema.org data, no per-product name/price/image. Most of the rest of the site is one-off named Kintsugi client commissions and repair supplies, not shop-able design objects. Real working London ceramicist (Mizuyo Yamashita), but nothing structured to scrape right now - worth rechecking later in case a real shop catalog appears.

name: Studio Racines
notes: Genuine Shopify storefront with a robots.txt that explicitly allows crawling (no bot-specific block) - but the whole site is currently behind Shopify's password/coming-soon gate (homepage and /collections/all both redirect to 'Enter using password', /products.json returns 401). Nothing public to scrape yet. Not excluded, just not launched - recheck once it's live.

name: e15
notes: robots.txt itself is permissive (no bot-specific block, just generic WP-admin/downloads/sample-sale exclusions). Magento catalog, real per-product data confirmed (its /en/all-products.html?limit=all listing briefly returned all 141 products with clean name/category/image in one fetch). But real bot-mitigation infrastructure kicked in during testing - the same URLs (and eventually the homepage too) started returning 403 consistently, including for a plain browser user-agent and curl, not just this scraper's own UA. Same treatment as Nikari's Cloudflare wall: not routed around.

name: De La Espada
notes: Genuine Shopify storefront, robots.txt allows crawling (Shopify's standard agentic-commerce template, no bot-specific block). 349 clean products across real categories (Sofas, Storage, Dining Chairs, etc.), no junk/sample/swatch categories found, all 349 have images - uses the existing generic extract_shopify unmodified. One small known gap: 8 of 349 products (2.3%) use ' - ' as part of their real name (e.g. 'TAI HEN - BOOKSHELF') rather than as a variant separator, so _base_name() truncates the descriptive suffix on display - not a merging/duplication bug, just a shortened name on a handful of cards.

name: Elliott Denny
notes: robots.txt blocks everything for every user-agent (User-agent: * / Disallow: /) - a blanket site-wide block including search engines, not just AI/bot crawlers. Clearest possible exclusion signal, no further checks needed.

name: Piet Hein Eek
notes: Real WooCommerce store, robots.txt is generic Yoast/WP boilerplate (no bot block). 1,141 raw products across 12 pages, uses the existing generic extract_woocommerce. Real per-brand quirk found and handled: several categories ('Architectuur', 'Architectuur projecten', 'Inrichtingen', 'Horeca', ~50-60 items) are real architecture/interior-fit-out case studies (hospitality venues, private homes), not purchasable furniture - confirmed all price=0 and added to EXCLUDED_CATEGORIES. Note most of the REAL flagship scrapwood ('Sloophout') pieces are also price=0 (priced on request, common for one-of-a-kind artisanal furniture) - price alone isn't a reliable signal here, category is. The much broader 'Opdrachten' (commissions) category was deliberately left alone - it mixes those same project writeups with genuinely real bespoke furniture, too broad to exclude cleanly.

name: Joris Poggioli
notes: No robots.txt file exists at all (site returns its own 404 page for the path) - no bot restrictions of any kind. Next.js app whose homepage server-renders its entire 74-item design catalog directly in a __NEXT_DATA__ JSON blob - name, category, material, dimensions, and image all present, no per-product fetch needed. The site's separate 'architecture' section (real interior/hospitality project case studies) isn't part of this data at all, so nothing to exclude.

name: Moustache
notes: PrestaShop store, generic robots.txt (no bot block). Real structural complexity found and handled: the site runs two parallel, near-non-overlapping category URL trees under /en/ (an older French-slugged one and a newer English-slugged one, most likely because English URL slugs were only set on newer categories) - no single 'all products' listing actually covers everything (its 86-all category is itself just a distinct 54-item subset). extract_moustache() fetches every real object-type category from both trees and dedupes by PrestaShop's own numeric product ID. Also found: each color is its own top-level product (confirmed live - 'Gelato chair' alone had 42 separate IDs, one per color, with the color name only appearing in the product URL's fragment, not the visible name) - 78% of the raw 444-item catalog was this pattern. Grouped by exact product name with colors parsed from the URL fragment into material_options, same treatment as every other brand's variant-duplication problem. 157 real products after grouping.
